contradictions.question: Who makes people blind?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 4:11 has Yahweh personally claim authorship over blindness, deafness, and muteness — they are direct acts of God. Mark 9:17-25, by contrast, treats deafness and muteness as the work of a foul spirit that Jesus exorcises, and John 9:1-3 treats congenital blindness as a setup for a divine demonstration rather than a curse to be undone. The Hebrew Bible's strict monotheistic etiology of disability collides with the Synoptic demonology that develops in the Second Temple period.
contradictions.commentary:
Here's the thing — Exodus 4:11 is unambiguous. Yahweh is asserting sole agency over sensory disability as part of his self-justification to Moses. The verb is qal active: "Who makes (sam) a person mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?" There's no demonic intermediary in the picture. The text reflects what John Collins calls the radically monistic theology of the priestly and Deuteronomistic traditions — Yahweh is the sole causal agent for both prosperity and calamity (cf. Isaiah 45:7, Amos 3:6).

By the time you get to Mark, the entire causal universe has been repopulated. Mark 9:25 explicitly names the spirit "deaf and dumb" (to alalon kai kophon pneuma) and commands it to leave — the disability is the spirit. This is straight Second Temple demonology, the kind you find in 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and the Qumran exorcism fragments. The apologist move here is to say these are separate cases — God causes some disabilities, demons cause others, and there's no contradiction. The apologist playbook, page one. The problem is that Exodus 4:11 is framed as a universal etiological claim, not a case-by-case attribution. Yahweh isn't saying "I make some blind people" — he's making a sweeping claim of authorship to ground Moses' commission.

The John 9:1-3 passage adds a third theological layer: blindness as a setup for divine theater. Raymond Brown notes that John pointedly rejects both Deuteronomic retributive justice (this man didn't sin, his parents didn't sin) and the Synoptic demonological frame — instead, blindness exists "so that the works of God might be revealed in him." That's a third etiology, not a harmonization. Three different theological universes, three different causal agents.

contradictions.question: How did Jesus cure the blind man?
contradictions.summary: Mark 8:22-25 has Jesus heal a blind man at Bethsaida by spitting directly on his eyes and laying hands on him — twice, because the first attempt only half-worked. John 9:1-7 has Jesus heal a blind man in Jerusalem by spitting on the ground, mixing clay, anointing the man's eyes, and sending him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. Different cities, different methods, different timeline, and a different number of steps. Apologists treat them as separate events; the literary parallels suggest John has reworked the Markan tradition into something more dignified.
contradictions.commentary:
At face value these are two different healings — different settings, different protagonists, different outcomes. Apologists like Craig Blomberg lean on this hard: no contradiction because no overlap. Fair enough as a first pass. But here's where it falls apart under scrutiny. The Mark 8 healing is the one synoptic miracle that John 9 is most plausibly transforming. Joel Marcus and Raymond Brown both note the structural parallels: spittle, hands, a two-stage process, a confession of sight. Mark's version is also the one healing the other synoptics conspicuously drop — Matthew and Luke both omit Mark 8:22-26, almost certainly because the two-stage failure and the saliva are theologically awkward. Jesus needing a second try is not a good look.

The parsimonious reading is that John 9 represents a Johannine reworking of the same tradition that produced Mark 8 — saliva is kept (it was too embedded to drop), but the messy two-stage healing is replaced with a single competent act mediated through the Pool of Siloam, which John then helpfully glosses as "Sent" (apestalmenos) — a symbol for Jesus himself. The apologist response — these are simply distinct miracles — has to explain why Jesus used the unusual saliva-and-mud technique twice, in two different cities, with no other healing in the Gospels resembling it. That's not impossible. It's just less parsimonious than the redactional explanation.

Even if you grant the two-event harmonization, the contradiction the SAB is pointing at is still there at the level of method: the Mark version cures by direct spittle on eyes, John cures by mud-paste and a pool washing. Same question — how does Jesus heal blindness? — and two non-overlapping answers. That is of course only a contradiction if you assume one consistent method, which the text never claims.

contradictions.question: Is it possible to fall from grace?
contradictions.summary: Galatians 5:4, Hebrews 6:4-6, and 2 Peter 2:20-21 all explicitly treat falling away from saving grace as possible — Hebrews even pronounces it irrevocable. John 10:28 and Romans 8:38-39 just as explicitly insist that nothing can separate believers from Christ's hand or God's love. This is the classic Reformed-vs-Arminian seam in the New Testament itself: two streams of soteriology that the canon never reconciles.
contradictions.commentary:
The two New Testament streams here aren't subtle. Hebrews 6:4-6 is some of the most explicit apostasy language in the canon: those once enlightened, who tasted the heavenly gift and shared in the Holy Spirit, who then fall away — adynaton, impossible to restore them. Galatians 5:4 uses the unambiguous exepesate — "you have fallen out of grace." 2 Peter 2:20-21 piles on with the line that it would have been better not to have known the way of righteousness than to know it and turn back. On the other side, John 10:28 has Jesus declaring no one can snatch his sheep from his hand, and Romans 8:38-39 stacks negation after negation: nothing in creation can separate us from God's love in Christ.

The apologist harmonization runs through two main moves. First — the Calvinist move (Schreiner, Grudem) — argue that the apostates in Hebrews and 2 Peter were never genuinely saved in the first place. They merely "tasted" without consuming. The problem is that the language Hebrews uses for these people (enlightened, partakers of the Holy Spirit, tasted the powers of the age to come) is precisely the language Hebrews uses elsewhere for true believers. The phrase phōtisthentas (enlightened) is technical baptismal vocabulary in early Christian usage. Second — the Arminian-leaning move (Witherington) — accept that apostasy is real and read John 10 and Romans 8 as referring to external threats, not internal defection. That's plausible for Romans 8 (the list is all external agents), but John 10:28's "they shall never perish" is unconditional on its face.

The parsimonious read is that the New Testament contains multiple soteriological traditions that don't fully cohere. Hebrews and 2 Peter come out of a community concerned with maintaining commitment under persecution; Johannine and Pauline assurance texts come out of communities emphasizing security in Christ. Both are real; neither is dominant. Take your pick on which to weight — the canon doesn't.

contradictions.question: Who sent the Holy Ghost?
contradictions.summary: In John 15:26 Jesus says he himself will send the Paraclete from the Father. In John 14:16 and 14:26 the Father is the one who gives or sends the Spirit, with Jesus only asking. The same Farewell Discourse, two chapters apart, gives two different agents for the same act — a tension that drove the *Filioque* controversy that split Eastern and Western Christianity for a thousand years.
contradictions.commentary:
This one isn't even cross-document — it's the same author, the same discourse, two chapters apart. John 14:16: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete." John 14:26: "the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name." John 15:26: "the Paraclete, whom I will send to you from the Father." The subject of the sending verb (pempso vs. pempsei) literally changes between verses.

The orthodox harmonization is Trinitarian: the Father is the ultimate source, the Son is the mediating sender, and there's no real conflict because the persons of the Trinity act inseparably (the doctrine of *opera trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt*). That's a perfectly coherent dogmatic position — but it's a fifth-century answer to a first-century problem. Raymond Brown, who was a Catholic priest and absolutely no anti-Trinitarian, still acknowledged in his Anchor Bible commentary that John's Spirit-language is ambiguous about agency and that the Farewell Discourse may reflect two stages of composition — chapters 15-17 likely being a later expansion of the original chapter 14 discourse.

The more interesting historical point is what this contradiction did downstream. The question of whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone (John 14:26) or from the Father and the Son (John 15:26) is exactly the *Filioque* clause — the Latin addition to the Nicene Creed that the Eastern Church rejected and that became the formal theological cause of the 1054 Great Schism. The contradiction is real enough that an entire half of Christendom built its identity on one reading and the other half on the other. You can call that a harmonized doctrine of Trinitarian co-agency, or you can call it two competing source layers in a composite discourse. The text itself does not adjudicate.

contradictions.question: Did any of the apostles ask Jesus where he was going?
contradictions.summary: In John 13:36 Peter explicitly asks Jesus, "Lord, where are you going?" Thomas asks essentially the same question in John 14:5. Then in John 16:5, Jesus says, "none of you asks me, where are you going?" — within the same Farewell Discourse. The Johannine author has Jesus deny that anyone has just asked him the question that two named disciples just asked him.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in the Gospel of John, and it's a major piece of evidence for the source-critical view that John 13-17 is a stitched-together composite. Peter in 13:36: *Kyrie, pou hypageis?* — "Lord, where are you going?" Thomas in 14:5: *Kyrie, ouk oidamen pou hypageis* — "Lord, we do not know where you are going." Jesus in 16:5: *oudeis ex hymōn erōta me, Pou hypageis?* — "none of you is asking me, where are you going?" The exact same phrase, *pou hypageis*, is the issue across all three.

The traditional apologetic harmonization (Carson, Morris) is to translate 16:5 as a present-tense observation — "none of you is asking *now*, in this moment," implying that the earlier questions were superficial and they've stopped asking because they're sad about the leaving. That reading is grammatically possible but contextually strained. Why would Jesus complain that they're not asking the question they did ask, while ignoring the fact that they asked it twice?

The parsimonious explanation is the one Raymond Brown, Rudolf Bultmann, and a broad swath of Johannine scholarship landed on: the Farewell Discourse is composite. The original discourse probably ended around 14:31 ("Rise, let us go from here") and chapters 15-17 are a later supplement by the Johannene community or redactor. Chapter 16 was likely composed without 13:36-14:5 in view, which is why it contradicts them. This is the same problem that produces the disconnect between 14:31's "let's leave" and the fact that they don't actually leave until 18:1. The apologist treats these as theological deepening; the critical reader treats them as seams. Take your pick — but the seams hypothesis explains the data without making Jesus contradict himself.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus tell his disciples everything?
contradictions.summary: In John 15:15 Jesus declares he has made known to his disciples "all things" he heard from the Father — the word is *panta*, everything. One chapter later, in John 16:12, he tells them he still has many things to say to them that they cannot bear right now. Same discourse, same audience, two flatly opposed claims about how much Jesus has communicated.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction lives in the same neighborhood as the previous one — the seams of the Johannine Farewell Discourse. John 15:15: *panta ha ēkousa para tou patros mou egnōrisa hymin* — "all things that I heard from my Father I have made known to you." That's a comprehensive claim. The Greek *panta* doesn't admit easy qualification — it means everything, the totality. Then John 16:12: *eti polla echō hymin legein, all' ou dynasthe bastazein arti* — "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now." The same speaker, two chapters later, says the opposite.

The standard apologetic move (Carson, Köstenberger) is to read *panta* in 15:15 as comprehensive only with respect to what Jesus has revealed about his identity and mission — everything *relevant*, not everything *possible*. Then 16:12 covers the additional revelation that will come through the Paraclete. That reading rescues the harmony at the cost of inserting a qualifier the text doesn't have. "All things" gets quietly converted into "all things in the relevant category," with the category supplied by the interpreter.

The critical reading, again, is compositional. C. K. Barrett and Raymond Brown both treated chapters 15-17 as a secondary expansion of an earlier discourse, with 16:12 written in a context where the focus had shifted to ongoing revelation through the Spirit — a Johannine community theologumenon about the Paraclete's continuing teaching role (cf. 16:13, "he will guide you into all truth"). The point of 16:12 in its own context isn't to undermine 15:15 — it's to legitimate the community's later teachings as Spirit-mediated extensions of what Jesus didn't get around to saying directly. That works just fine as a Johannine theological move, but it does contradict the prior claim in 15:15. The contradiction is the cost of stitching the two layers together.

contradictions.question: Was Mary Magdalene happy or sad when she saw the risen Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:1-9 has the women — including Mary Magdalene — leave the empty tomb with "fear and great joy," meet Jesus on the way, grab his feet, and worship. John 20:11-15 has Mary Magdalene weeping at the tomb, talking to angels through tears, and failing even to recognize Jesus when he stands in front of her, mistaking him for the gardener. The emotional state, the location of the encounter, and her ability to recognize him are all different.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard apologist move (Wenham, Licona) is sequential reconstruction: Mary Magdalene came to the tomb, ran to tell the disciples (John 20:1-2), then came back and had the weeping encounter (John 20:11-15), while in between or simultaneously the other women had the joyful Matthew 28 encounter. That can be made to work if you assume two trips and split the women up, but it requires importing scaffolding that none of the Gospels supply.

The real problem isn't the emotional state by itself — people can shift moods — but the recognition failure in John. *dokousa hoti ho kēpouros estin* — "thinking that he is the gardener." This is theologically loaded in John: Mary recognizes Jesus only when he speaks her name (John 20:16, *Mariam*), which is John's payoff of the shepherd-knows-his-sheep-by-name theme from chapter 10. The recognition failure is not incidental. It's doing theological work in John's narrative. Matthew's version, where the women immediately recognize him and grab his feet, doesn't need any such moment because Matthew is doing different theological work — vindicating Jesus' messianic authority through the women's worship.

Dale Allison's three-volume Matthew commentary points out that the resurrection appearances are the area of greatest divergence across the Gospels and the most likely candidates for late, theologically-shaped additions. The Markan account in its original ending (16:8) has the women fleeing in fear and saying nothing to anyone. Matthew adds Jesus' actual appearance; John adds an entire scene with angels, weeping, gardener-confusion, and the noli me tangere moment. These aren't supplementary details fitting into one timeline — they're competing narrative theologies. The honest critical read is that the resurrection traditions diversified rapidly in the first generation and the Gospels preserved different versions without successful harmonization.

contradictions.question: Should we believe in unseen things?
contradictions.summary: Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as the evidence of things not seen; 2 Corinthians 4:18 says we look at things unseen rather than seen; 2 Corinthians 5:7 — "we walk by faith, not by sight"; John 20:29 has Jesus pronouncing those who believe without seeing as blessed. Colossians 2:18, by contrast, warns against being beguiled by people "intruding into those things which they have not seen, vainly puffed up by their fleshly mind." The same New Testament both commands and condemns belief in the unseen, depending on whose visions are being weighed.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a contradiction that mostly evaporates with a careful look at Colossians 2:18 — but only partly. The Greek of Colossians 2:18 is famously contested. The phrase *ha heoraken embateuōn* is variously translated "intruding into things he has seen" (taking the manuscript reading without the negative) or "intruding into things he has not seen" (with the negative *mē*, attested in some manuscripts and reflected in the KJV). The earlier and better attested reading is *without* the negative — so the verse is actually criticizing people who claim to have seen visions during their initiation into some Colossian mystery cult and then puff themselves up about it. The KJV's negative reading flips the meaning and is what creates the surface contradiction the SAB is pointing to.

So if you grant that the modern critical text wins on Colossians 2:18, the contradiction with Hebrews 11 dissolves in one direction — Colossians isn't actually condemning belief in unseen things; it's criticizing people who claim privileged visionary access. That's a textual-criticism point, not a theological one.

But the deeper tension is still real and worth flagging. The New Testament does treat "faith without sight" as the higher virtue (John 20:29, Hebrews 11) while at the same time grounding apostolic authority in eyewitness claims (1 John 1:1, Luke 1:2, 1 Corinthians 15:5-8, 2 Peter 1:16). Bart Ehrman has pointed out that this is the structural irony of early Christianity — eyewitnesses are normative for the apostles, and lack of sight is normative for everyone after them. The contradiction here is between the early-stage epistemology (visions, appearances) and the later-stage epistemology (faith without sight). The SAB pairing is too narrow to catch the full tension, but it's pointing at a real seam. That is of course only a contradiction if you read these as competing universal claims, which the texts arguably don't.

contradictions.question: Did Luke include everything that Jesus did?
contradictions.summary: Acts 1:1-2 opens with Luke telling Theophilus that his "former treatise" (the Gospel of Luke) covered "all that Jesus began both to do and teach" up to the ascension. John 21:25 ends by claiming the things Jesus did were so many that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written. The contradiction is a soft one — Luke's *panta* (all) versus John's hyperbolic inexhaustibility — and depends on whether you read Acts 1:1 as a literal completeness claim or as a conventional preface.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the weaker contradictions in the SAB collection, and it's worth saying so plainly. Acts 1:1 reads: *peri pantōn, ō Theophile, hōn ērxato ho Iēsous poiein te kai didaskein* — "concerning all the things, O Theophilus, that Jesus began both to do and to teach." The key word is *ērxato* (began). Luke is signaling that the Gospel covers what Jesus *began* doing, and that Acts will narrate the continuation through the Spirit and the apostles. The grammar already softens the totality claim. Joseph Fitzmyer in his Anchor Bible Acts commentary takes this as a standard hellenistic preface convention, comparable to Josephus and Lucian — not a literal claim of exhaustiveness.

John 21:25 is doing different work entirely. It's a literary peroration, hyperbole built into the closing of the Gospel: "if every one of them were written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books." Raymond Brown points out this is a standard Hellenistic literary topos — Philo, Quintilian, and various rabbinic sources use the same "the world could not contain it" trope. It's signaling literary closure, not making a claim that competes with Luke's preface.

So here's the honest assessment. If you read Acts 1:1's *peri pantōn* maximally and John 21:25 literally, you get a surface contradiction. If you read both verses in their actual literary register — Luke as preface convention, John as closing hyperbole — they're not really claiming the same kind of thing. This entry is closer to a translation-driven artifact than a genuine doctrinal collision. That is of course a subjective call, but the weight of Acts and Johannine scholarship leans toward both phrases being literary rather than catalog claims. Keep the entry, but flag it as one where the harmonization is genuinely strong on textual grounds.

contradictions.question: How many believers were there at the time of the ascension?
contradictions.summary: Acts 1:15 reports the number of names "together" right after the ascension as "about one hundred and twenty." Paul, writing decades earlier in 1 Corinthians 15:6, says the risen Jesus appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom were still alive when he wrote. If both numbers are accurate, more than 380 named believers vanished from the Jerusalem community between the resurrection and the post-ascension prayer gathering.
contradictions.commentary:
Here's where the apologetic harmonization actually has some traction — and where it ultimately runs out of road. The standard move (F. F. Bruce, Bock) is geographic and demographic: the 120 in Acts 1:15 are specifically the believers gathered in one room in Jerusalem in the days immediately after the ascension. The 500-plus appearance witnesses of 1 Corinthians 15:6 likely happened in Galilee (cf. Matthew 28:16-20, the Galilean commissioning) and they all went home. So the two numbers refer to different geographic snapshots, and there's no contradiction.

That's plausible as far as it goes. The problem is what it costs to make it work. You have to accept that of more than 500 people who personally saw the risen Jesus — the most extraordinary thing they'd ever experienced — fewer than 120 followed through to join the Jerusalem community at the founding moment of the church. That's a roughly 75% attrition rate among eyewitnesses. The Acts narrative itself doesn't seem aware that there are hundreds of other resurrection witnesses scattered around Galilee; the framing of Pentecost in Acts 2 treats the 120 as the core community, not as a Jerusalem subset of a much larger witness pool.

The parsimonious read, on the critical side (Lüdemann, Ehrman), is that Paul's "500 at once" is either an embellishment, a reference to a mass ecstatic experience after the fact, or simply a number Paul could not have independently verified. Note that the 500 appearance appears nowhere in the Gospels or Acts. If 500 people had seen the risen Jesus, you'd expect at least one of the Gospel writers to know about it. That gap is hard to explain on the harmonization view. The apologist can keep both numbers if they're willing to accept the 75% attrition. The critical scholar reads the gap as evidence that the 500-witness tradition was a Pauline-circulated claim that didn't propagate into the Gospel-Acts stream.

contradictions.question: What did Judas do with the silver?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 27:5 has Judas throw the thirty pieces of silver down in the temple and then hang himself; the priests use the money to buy the Potter's Field. Acts 1:18 says Judas himself bought a field with the reward of iniquity and then fell headlong, bursting open with his bowels gushing out. Same character, same money, two incompatible accounts of who bought what field and how Judas died.
contradictions.commentary:
This one is famous, and the harmonization attempts are creative — and inadequate. The Matthew version: Judas regrets, returns the silver, hangs himself; priests buy the Potter's Field with the now-blood-money. Acts version: Judas keeps the money, buys a field himself, and dies by some kind of bodily rupture (*prēnēs genomenos elakēsen mesos*).

The traditional apologist move (Archer, Geisler) tries to fuse the two: Judas bought the field via the priests as proxy, then hanged himself, and the rope broke or the body decomposed and burst open after falling. So both accounts are partially true. The problems here stack up fast. First, Matthew explicitly says the priests bought the field with the money — *agorazein* — there's no agency or proxy language. Second, Acts says Judas "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity" — that's direct action, not posthumous attribution. Third, the burst-open-after-hanging reconciliation requires inventing a chain of events neither text describes. Fourth, even the name of the field differs in implication: Matthew calls it Field of Blood because it was bought with blood money; Acts calls it Field of Blood (Hakeldama) because Judas's blood burst out on it. Same name, different etiology.

Dale Allison and Joseph Fitzmyer both treat this as two independent legendary developments of an early tradition that linked Judas's death to a piece of land near Jerusalem. Matthew is doing fulfillment work — the thirty pieces of silver, the potter's field, the blood money — all dovetailing with Zechariah 11:12-13 and Jeremiah 18-19 (which Matthew misattributes to Jeremiah at 27:9). Acts is doing typological work — Judas as the wicked man whose body explodes is a riff on Wisdom 4:19 and Psalm 69:25 (cited at Acts 1:20). Neither is reporting; both are theologizing. The apologist harmonization fails because it tries to read two competing midrashic etiologies as overlapping eyewitness reports. They are not. Take your pick on which Judas-death tradition you find more compelling — but you cannot have both as straight history.

contradictions.question: Who raised Jesus from the dead?
contradictions.summary: John 2:19-21 has Jesus declaring he will raise his own body in three days. Acts 2:24, 2:32, 4:10, 13:30, Galatians 1:1, Colossians 2:12, and 1 Thessalonians 1:10 all attribute the resurrection to God the Father, who raised Jesus. Romans 8:11 attributes it to the Holy Spirit. Three different agents across the New Testament for the same act, with the bulk of attestation going to the Father.
contradictions.commentary:
The orthodox harmonization is straightforward Trinitarian theology: all three persons act inseparably, and the resurrection is the work of the one God in three persons. That's a perfectly fine confessional answer, and it works on the dogmatic level. The historical-critical question is different — namely, what did the earliest Christians actually think happened, and did they think the same thing?

When you sort the verses chronologically you see something interesting. The earliest stratum — Paul's undisputed letters and the speeches in Acts (which preserve early creedal material) — overwhelmingly attribute the resurrection to God the Father acting on Jesus. *Ho theos auton ēgeiren ek nekrōn* ("God raised him from the dead") is one of the most common formulas in the New Testament. Jesus is the patient, God is the agent. This fits the early christological pattern that Bart Ehrman calls "exaltation Christology" — Jesus is a man whom God vindicated and exalted by raising him.

The John 2:19-21 saying — Jesus actively raising himself — is a Johannine theological development that aligns with John's high Christology of the pre-existent Logos. Even there, the narrator has to clarify that Jesus "spoke of the temple of his body," because the saying in its original form (cf. Mark 14:58, where the temple-destruction saying is preserved without the self-raising element) didn't necessarily imply self-resurrection. Romans 8:11 is the Spirit-resurrection tradition, which is rarer and appears to be a Pauline pneumatological emphasis rather than a developed doctrine.

The parsimonious read is developmental: the earliest formula is "God raised Jesus," the Pauline Spirit-formula is a side variant, and the Johannine self-raising formula is the latest theological refinement, made possible only after the Logos Christology was in place. You can call that a Trinitarian harmony retroactively, or you can call it three stages of Christological development. The data is the same; the interpretive frame is what changes.

contradictions.question: Should we obey human or divine law?
contradictions.summary: Acts 5:29 has Peter and the apostles declaring before the Sanhedrin that they must obey God rather than men. 1 Peter 2:13 commands believers to submit to every human ordinance, and Romans 13:1-4 escalates: every governing authority is ordained by God, resisting them resists God, and they bear the sword as God's ministers to execute wrath. The same New Testament endorses both civil disobedience and unconditional submission, depending on which book you're reading.
contradictions.commentary:
The standard harmonization is the so-called "two kingdoms" or hierarchical reading: obey civil authorities in all matters where their commands don't violate divine law; obey God when they do. That's a perfectly coherent ethical framework, and it's the dominant Christian reading from Augustine through the Reformers. The problem is that this framework has to be imported from outside the texts — neither Romans 13 nor 1 Peter 2 carves out exceptions for unjust commands. Romans 13:1-2 is categorical: every soul to the higher powers, no exceptions stated. *Pasa psychē exousiais hyperechousais hypotassesthō* — "let every soul be subject to the governing authorities." Paul gives no "unless they command sin" qualifier.

Acts 5:29, by contrast, is the apostles directly defying a legitimate authority — the Sanhedrin had authority over Jewish religious matters, and Peter is openly refusing to comply. If Romans 13 is the rule, Acts 5:29 is the exception that Romans 13 doesn't acknowledge. The clean reading is that these are different theological streams responding to different situations. Romans was written to a Roman-Christian community in the imperial capital where political quietism was survival strategy. 1 Peter addresses scattered Christians under imperial pressure with similar concerns. Acts 5:29 is hagiographic — Luke is establishing the apostles as figures of conscience who stand up to corrupt authority. Each text is doing different rhetorical work for different audiences.

The contradiction has had massive downstream effects. Romans 13 has been deployed by every authoritarian Christian regime from Constantine to apartheid South Africa to Trump-era evangelicalism (cf. Jeff Sessions' 2018 invocation to justify family separation). Acts 5:29 is the standard text for Christian civil disobedience from the Anabaptists to Martin Luther King Jr. The New Testament hands the ethical question to the reader without giving them the resolution rules. Take your pick on which verse anchors your political theology — both have impeccable apostolic credentials.

contradictions.question: How old was Abraham when he left Haran?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 12:4 says Abram was 75 years old when he departed Haran. Genesis 11:26 says Terah was 70 when he begat Abram; Genesis 11:32 says Terah died at 205. Acts 7:2-4 explicitly says Abraham left Haran only after Terah died. Doing the arithmetic — 205 minus 70 — Terah died when Abram was 135. The Genesis 11 chronology combined with Stephen's speech in Acts is incompatible with Genesis 12:4.
contradictions.commentary:
The arithmetic here is unforgiving and the contradiction is mechanical. Genesis 11:26 — Terah begat Abram at 70. Genesis 11:32 — Terah dies at 205. Subtraction: Abram is 135 when Terah dies. Acts 7:4 — Abram leaves Haran *after* Terah dies. Genesis 12:4 — Abram leaves Haran at 75. 75 does not equal 135.

The standard apologist resolution, which goes back to Augustine and is endorsed by Gleason Archer, takes Genesis 11:26 as a summary statement that doesn't mean Abram was Terah's firstborn. The reasoning: Genesis 11:26 says "Terah lived 70 years and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran" — three sons listed, not all necessarily born when Terah was 70. Abram is listed first because of his theological importance, not birth order. So Abram could actually have been born when Terah was 130, making him 75 when Terah died at 205. The same move is made in Genesis 5 and 10.

This works as a textual maneuver but it's strained. The Hebrew construction of Genesis 11:26 follows the pattern of all the other patriarchal birth notices in chapter 11 — "X lived Y years and begat Z" — and in every other case the begetting age refers to the named child. The apologetic reading has to make Genesis 11:26 uniquely a summary statement while every other case in the chapter is direct. That's special pleading. The harder problem is Acts 7:4 itself. Stephen's speech reflects a tradition (likely from Philo or a similar Second Temple Jewish reading) that explicitly placed Abraham's departure after Terah's death. Stephen and the Genesis 12:4 chronology are operating from different starting assumptions.

The critical consensus, going back to Wellhausen and modern Pentateuchal scholars like Joel Baden, is that the Abraham chronology in Genesis was assembled from P-source genealogies and J-source narrative, and the seams between sources produced the inconsistency. Acts 7 then preserves a separate Hellenistic Jewish tradition that aligned with one possible reading but not with Genesis 12:4 as it stands. Three traditions, no clean fit. Take your pick — but the math is what it is.

contradictions.question: Did Paul go to Jerusalem from Damascus immediately after his conversion?
contradictions.summary: Acts 9:26 says that when Saul came to Jerusalem after his conversion he tried to join the disciples, and the Lukan narrative places this trip very close to the Damascus event. Galatians 1:16-17, written by Paul himself, flatly denies it: he says immediately after his calling he did *not* go up to Jerusalem to confer with anyone, but went into Arabia and back to Damascus first, only going up to Jerusalem three years later (1:18). Luke and Paul tell incompatible stories about the post-conversion trajectory.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest test cases for the historical reliability of Acts versus the autobiographical claims in Paul's own letters — and it's one where most critical scholars side with Paul. Paul writes Galatians under oath, essentially, swearing he's not lying (Gal 1:20). He's making his point precisely because his apostolic legitimacy depends on his not having received his gospel from the Jerusalem pillars. His own credibility on the timeline is staked on the claim that he didn't go up to Jerusalem immediately. He went to Arabia. Then back to Damascus. Then, *meta etē tria* — after three years — he went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, for just fifteen days, and saw no other apostle except James the Lord's brother (Gal 1:18-19).

Acts 9:26 places Saul's arrival in Jerusalem after he escapes Damascus by being lowered in a basket (Acts 9:25), which Acts treats as immediately following the conversion. Acts knows nothing of the Arabian sojourn. The Lukan timeline runs: conversion → Damascus preaching → escape → Jerusalem.

The traditional apologetic harmonization (Bruce, Witherington) inserts the Arabian trip into the gap implied by Acts 9:23 ("after many days") and treats Luke's "many days" as accommodating the three years. That works as a smoothing exercise, but it requires reading Acts 9:23-26 as a heavily compressed summary that silently skips an entire multi-year Arabian and Damascene ministry. The narrative as Luke tells it gives no indication of that compression.

The critical consensus, from Ernst Haenchen forward, is that Luke either didn't know about the Arabian period or chose to omit it because it didn't fit his theological program of presenting Paul as quickly integrated into the apostolic community. Luke is doing the work of harmonizing Paul with the Jerusalem mother church; Paul is doing the work of insisting on his independence from it. Different agendas, different timelines. Paul's first-person account wins on direct evidentiary grounds. Acts is doing apologetic narration. Take your pick on which to trust, but the methodological default in critical scholarship is to weight the primary source over the secondary.

contradictions.question: Is circumcision required?
contradictions.summary: The question header asks about circumcision, but the proof-texts cited concern food offered to idols, not circumcision. 1 Corinthians 8:4-8 says food doesn't commend us to God; Acts 15:28-29 records the Jerusalem Council prohibiting Gentile believers from eating food offered to idols. The cited verses point to a real contradiction — Paul vs. the Jerusalem Council on idol-meat — but the question label is wrong. This is a mis-titled entry.
contradictions.commentary:
PRELIM FLAG: The question text and the cited verses don't match. The question asks whether circumcision is required; the verses are about food offered to idols. The questionUrl points to /contra/meat.html — "meat" — which is the SAB's actual category. The SAB entry is really about food sacrificed to idols, and the question title in this database is mis-labeled. That mismatch needs human correction at the database level.

That said, the underlying contradiction the verses are pointing at is real and worth describing. 1 Corinthians 8:4-8: Paul argues that since idols are nothing, meat sacrificed to them is theologically neutral; eating it neither commends nor condemns. The only constraint is not to scandalize a weaker brother whose conscience is troubled. Acts 15:28-29: the Jerusalem Council under James decrees that Gentile believers must abstain from meat sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality. These are presented as binding (*epanankes* — "necessary").

Paul's stance in 1 Corinthians 8-10 (cf. Romans 14) treats the idol-meat question as a matter of Christian liberty conditioned only by love for the weaker member. The Jerusalem Council treats it as a categorical prohibition. F. F. Bruce and the conservative tradition try to reconcile these by reading the Acts 15 decree as a temporary local accommodation for Antioch and Asia Minor, not a universal mandate — and noting that Paul might have respected the decree in those areas while teaching liberty elsewhere. But Paul never references the Jerusalem decree in his letters, including in 1 Corinthians, where it would have settled the dispute. Paul's silence on the Apostolic Decree (Acts 15) is one of the most consistent indicators that either Luke composed the decree to harmonize the early church or Paul didn't consider himself bound by it. The critical consensus (Lüdemann, Dunn) is that Luke's Acts 15 is a theological reconstruction; the historical Paul taught liberty on this question without conditions.

The SAB entry, once you correct the question title, is pointing at a real seam between Pauline and Lukan accounts of early church teaching.

contradictions.question: If a husband believes, is his wife saved also?
contradictions.summary: 1 Corinthians 7:14 says the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the believing one; Acts 16:31 promises the Philippian jailer that he and his household will be saved through his belief. 1 Corinthians 7:16 — written by the same Paul, in the same chapter — asks rhetorically, "How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?" The same author makes two opposite claims about the soteriological reach of one believing spouse, within the span of two verses.
contradictions.commentary:
This one is interesting because the contradiction lives in the same chapter, two verses apart. 1 Corinthians 7:14 — *hēgiastai gar ho anēr ho apistos en tē gynaiki* — "the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the wife." That's a present perfect — already accomplished, already a settled status. Then 7:16 — *ti gar oidas, gynai, ei ton andra sōseis?* — "how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?" Doubt, contingency, uncertainty. Same chapter, same Paul.

The standard exegetical move (Fee, Garland) distinguishes *hagiasmos* (sanctification, ritual/relational holiness) from *sōtēria* (salvation, eschatological deliverance). 7:14 is making the lesser claim — the unbelieving spouse is in some relational sense holy because of the believing spouse, making the marriage and children legitimate within the community. 7:16 is making the larger claim — whether the believing spouse will actually convert the unbeliever to faith remains uncertain. On this reading, sanctification and salvation are two different things, and there's no contradiction.

That distinction works exegetically. The catch is that Paul uses the same word-family elsewhere (*hēgiasmenoi* in 1 Cor 1:2; *hagiazō* throughout) for the soteriological status of believers, not just for relational holiness. The line between sanctification and salvation is blurry in Pauline thought, and 7:14 explicitly extends this status to the children: "else were your children unclean, but now are they holy." If the children are holy on account of one believing parent, that's pretty close to the inherited-salvation claim of Acts 16:31 ("believe and you will be saved, you and your household" — *sōthēsē sy kai ho oikos sou*).

Acts 16:31 is the bigger problem for the apologist. It explicitly promises salvation, not sanctification, to the jailer's household on the strength of his belief. That cuts against the standard Protestant individualist soteriology that requires each person to believe for themselves. The Reformed harmonization is to read "household" as meaning "each member who believes," but that's not what the Greek says. The text says *you and your household will be saved* on the basis of your belief. Compare 1 Cor 7:16 again: how do you know if you'll save your spouse? You don't. Take your pick — sanctification or salvation, household-grace or individual-grace. Paul and Luke aren't fully aligned.

contradictions.question: Can women be church leaders?
contradictions.summary: Acts 18:26 has Priscilla (with her husband Aquila) instructing Apollos in "the way of God" — a clear example of a woman exercising teaching authority in the early church. 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 commands that women keep silent in the churches and not speak; 1 Timothy 2:11-12 prohibits women from teaching or having authority over a man. Pauline-attributed texts both permit and prohibit female leadership in the same canon.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the contradictions where the critical-scholarly explanation is overwhelming and the apologetic explanation is fragile. 1 Timothy is not from Paul — the Pastoral Epistles (1-2 Timothy, Titus) are pseudepigraphic in the mainstream critical consensus, going back through Bauckham, Brown, and Ehrman. The vocabulary, the church-order concerns (overseers, deacons, widow lists), the polemic against "myths and endless genealogies," and the institutional setting all point to a late first or early second century author writing in Paul's name. So when 1 Timothy 2:11-12 prohibits women teaching, it's not Paul making that prohibition — it's a later Pauline-school author trying to constrain a Pauline tradition that had been more egalitarian.

1 Corinthians 14:34-35 is a different problem. Many critical scholars (Fee, Conzelmann, Ehrman) argue these verses are an interpolation. They interrupt the flow of Paul's argument about prophecy, they appear in different positions in some manuscripts (after 14:40 in the Western text tradition), and they directly contradict 1 Corinthians 11:5, where Paul assumes women are prophesying and praying in the assembly — he just wants them to do it with their heads covered. The textual evidence is suggestive enough that NA28 and several major critical commentaries treat 14:34-35 as possibly secondary.

Meanwhile, the egalitarian side of the canon is robust. Romans 16 names Phoebe as a deacon (*diakonos*) and Junia as outstanding among the apostles. Priscilla is consistently named before her husband Aquila — unusual in the ancient world and suggesting her prominence. Galatians 3:28 — neither male nor female in Christ — is a baptismal formula Paul cites approvingly. The apologist (Köstenberger, Schreiner) tries to reconcile by limiting the egalitarian texts to specific contexts and giving the restrictive texts universal force. The critical reading reverses that: the egalitarian practice is original, and the restrictive texts are either interpolations or pseudepigraphic walk-backs. Take your pick on which Paul to follow — but the historical Paul looks a lot more like the one who worked with Priscilla and Junia than the one who silences women in 1 Timothy.

contradictions.question: In whose name is baptism to be performed?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:19 has the risen Jesus command baptism "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" — a Trinitarian formula. Acts 2:38, 8:16, 10:48, and 19:5 all describe actual baptisms being performed in the name of Jesus Christ alone. The Lukan record of early church practice and the Matthean Great Commission disagree about the baptismal formula.
contradictions.commentary:
Here's where the textual history gets interesting. Every actual baptism described in Acts uses a Jesus-only formula — *eis to onoma tou kyriou Iēsou*, "in the name of the Lord Jesus," or variations. Four separate instances, all consistent. Matthew 28:19, by contrast, has the full Trinitarian formula — *eis to onoma tou patros kai tou hyiou kai tou hagiou pneumatos*. If the Great Commission as recorded in Matthew is what Jesus actually said, the apostles in Acts are systematically disobeying it.

The critical-scholarly explanation has two layers. First — and this is a longstanding minority position with serious advocates — there's textual evidence that the Trinitarian formula in Matthew 28:19 may be a later liturgical addition. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing before the Council of Nicaea, repeatedly quotes Matthew 28:19 in a shorter form: "Go and make disciples of all nations in my name." He cites this short form at least 17 times across his works. After Nicaea, Eusebius starts quoting the Trinitarian form. F. C. Conybeare argued in 1901 that the Trinitarian formula was a post-Nicene liturgical insertion. The textual evidence is contested — every Greek manuscript we have includes the Trinitarian formula — but Eusebius is an early and important witness, and his pre-Nicene quotations are weird.

Second — even if Matthew 28:19 is original in the Trinitarian form — the formula reflects the developed liturgical practice of Matthew's community at the time of writing (likely 80s-90s CE), not the historical practice of the earliest church. Acts preserves the older Jesus-only formula because that's what the early Christians actually did. Larry Hurtado and James Dunn both treat the Jesus-only baptism as the original practice; Matthew's Trinitarian formula reflects a later catechetical and liturgical development.

The apologist harmonization (Carson) reads "in the name of" as functionally equivalent across both formulations — the Jesus-only baptism is implicitly Trinitarian because Jesus is the second person of the Trinity. That's anachronistic theology imported into pre-Nicene texts. Take your pick — either Matthew 28:19 is a liturgical anachronism on the lips of Jesus, or the apostles systematically disobeyed his explicit command. Neither answer is comfortable for the harmonization view.

contradictions.question: Did the men with Paul hear the voice?
contradictions.summary: Acts 9:7 says the men traveling with Saul stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Acts 22:9 — in Paul's own retelling of the same event later in Acts — says they saw the light but did *not* hear the voice of the one speaking to him. Same author, same event, two flatly contradictory descriptions of what Saul's companions experienced. The reference "Acts.22:9" in the source uses a non-standard formatting (period instead of space).
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest in-canon contradictions because it's the same author contradicting himself about the same event. Acts 9:7: *akouontes men tēs phōnēs, mēdena de theōrountes* — "hearing the voice but seeing no one." Acts 22:9: *tēn de phōnēn ouk ēkousan tou lalountos moi* — "they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me." Both verses are Luke writing, both verses describe the Damascus road experience, and they directly disagree.

The traditional harmonization, going back to Augustine and championed by Gleason Archer, hinges on the Greek genitive vs. accusative distinction with *akouō*. *Akouō* + genitive (Acts 9:7, *tēs phōnēs*, genitive) supposedly means "hear a sound"; *akouō* + accusative (Acts 22:9, *tēn phōnēn*, accusative) supposedly means "hear with comprehension." So the men heard a sound but didn't understand the words. Problem solved.

This is one of the most repeated apologetic moves on this contradiction, and it doesn't survive scrutiny. The genitive/accusative distinction with *akouō* doesn't consistently work that way in Koine Greek. Daniel Wallace's *Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics* notes that the case distinction with *akouō* is not a reliable marker of comprehension vs. mere hearing. Examples cut both ways — accusative is used for unintelligible sounds, genitive for intelligible speech, and vice versa. F. F. Bruce, who is no friend to skeptical readings, admitted that the case-distinction harmonization "cannot be relied upon."

More importantly, the visual experience also contradicts. Acts 9:7 says they saw no one. Acts 22:9 says they saw the light. Acts 26:13-14 (Paul's third retelling) says everyone fell to the ground; Acts 9:7 says they stood. Three retellings, three different versions of who was standing, who fell, who saw what, who heard what. The critical consensus, from Haenchen forward, is that Luke is composing the three retellings independently for narrative purposes, not preserving a single eyewitness account. The discrepancies are exactly what you'd expect from an author writing dramatic speeches in character without harmonizing them against each other. Take your pick on which retelling counts — but the case-grammar dodge is dead.
